title: Agents That Write Their Own Tools at Runtime — Sandhya Subramani, AWS
description:
This agent starts with zero tools. Ask it for something it can't do, and it writes the tool and uses it without restarting.

Sandhya Subramani, senior developer advocate for GenAI at AWS, demos meta-tooling with the open-source Strands Agents SDK. That means agents that write, load and use their own tools at runtime, and even spin up their own sub-agents. All it takes is a system prompt describing what a good tool looks like, plus three tools: editor, shell and load_tool. She walks through agentic patterns (swarm, graph, handoff, workflow), demos a travel planner that builds its own sub-agents, and covers the evals and guardrails you need before trusting a self-modifying agent in production.

In this talk:
• Meta-tooling: editor, shell and load_tool plus one system prompt
• Agents that create their own sub-agents
• Evals for self-modifying agents: goal success, tool choice, parameters, inter-agent flow
• Guardrails: sandboxed execution, constrained permissions and observability

title: The Human Is an Async API — Melanie Warrick, Temporal
description:
Humans don't respond in 200 milliseconds. Your agent shouldn't fall over waiting for one.

Melanie Warrick from developer relations at Temporal shows how to build human-in-the-loop agents that don't block or lose state. Using a live multi-agent ice cream delivery demo with fleet, customer and dispatch agents on Google ADK and LangGraph, she explains why durability belongs in the agent harness and how Temporal's workers, workflows and activities track state. She shows how two primitives, a wait condition and a signal, let an agent pause for a human for minutes or weeks. Then she kills the worker mid-approval and brings it back with no lost work.

In this talk:
• Why a blocking 'ask the human' call breaks in production
• Temporal's workers, workflows and activities, and where model and tool calls belong
• Wait conditions and signals for human-to-agent and agent-to-human flows
• Deciding when a human should be in the loop: the cost of being wrong vs alert fatigue

title: Use ChatGPT to Break Tasks Into Steps Under 10 Minutes
description:
Follow me and DM me "PRACTICAL" on IG/FB only 👇

How to use AI to stop procrastinating...

You don't need a secret morning routine or another app. When a project feels too big, shrink the commitment until the first action feels easier to start.

Open ChatGPT or Claude and paste:

“I need to finish this thing but I keep avoiding it. Break it down into tiny actions, each one less than 10 minutes. Tell me the first, then wait until I’m done.”

Do only the first action. The goal isn't to finish the whole project in one session. The goal is to begin with a task small enough to complete in less than 10 minutes.

When you finish, take a break. Return to the same chat and say you're done. Then start the next action, which should also take less than 10 minutes.

Keep the AI focused on one action at a time. Don't ask for a giant plan and stare at the whole list. Let it give you the first action, wait for your update, then give you the next one.

This turns “finish the entire project” into one immediate step. Choose the task you've been avoiding, paste the prompt, and do the first action before planning anything else.

title: Tokenmaxxers Optimize the Wrong Thing
description:
Don't be a tokenmaxxer...

Tokenmaxxers chase the perfect prompt, squeeze every token, and switch between Claude and ChatGPT to stay on whichever model tech Twitter calls best.

None of those choices guarantees more progress. A more optimized model doesn't choose the right business problem for you.

Start with the highest-ROI business problem in front of you. Ask which problem, if solved today, would move the business forward. Then bring AI into the work.

Use AI to brainstorm possible approaches. Use it to plan the steps. Keep the problem at the center while you compare ideas and decide what to do next.

You don't need the perfect prompt for every task. You don't need to maximize every token. You don't need to change models whenever a new recommendation appears.

Prompt quality, token usage, and model choice still matter. They come after you choose a business problem worth solving. Start with the problem, then use ChatGPT or Claude to think and plan.
